sections.name: I-01 · fail · Consent treated as a one-time event

stickies.text:
I-01 · FAIL
Consent treated as a one-time event

Consent is treated as a one-time event, but participants' right to withdraw data later remains unresolved.

FAIL · bad_citation
nonexistent turns=[]; evidence_count=0

FAIL · unsupported
No turns are cited at all (evidence/sources empty), so the claim cannot be verified. Additionally, the claim that 'the right to withdraw remains unresolved' as a blanket statement ignores that several participants describe active, if imperfect, solutions to this exact problem (e.g. jamie discusses working with a colleague on a 'right to be forgotten' clause and ongoing dynamic consent; david describes continuous reminders and re-confirmation of consent throughout the project). The insight should be evidenced and should acknowledge these emerging practices rather than presenting the issue as wholly unaddressed.

turns: jamie:0024, david:0030, david:0034

sections.name: I-03 · fail · Depositing data feels like relational betrayal

stickies.text:
I-03 · FAIL
Depositing data feels like relational betrayal

Depositing data in archives can feel like betraying the researcher-participant relationship.

FAIL · bad_citation
nonexistent turns=[]; evidence_count=0

FAIL · unsupported
No turns cited. The specific framing 'relational betrayal' does not closely match what any participant said. The closest source is michelle, who describes the loss of a co-created 'partnership' and discomfort about ethics of relinquishing shared knowledge, but she does not describe it as 'betrayal' and this is a single-participant view being generalized into a field-wide insight.

turns: michelle:0040, michelle:0042

FAIL · missing_counterexample
This insight presents a single participant's (michelle's) framing as a general finding without noting that several other participants explicitly reject this framing: lisa argues that NOT sharing data, given her participants' desire for exposure, would be 'a disservice' to them; ana's participants asked for reciprocity via publication; jessica and kelly frame open deposit as fulfilling a duty to participants, not betraying them. This is a significant, easily-findable counter-perspective that should be surfaced.

turns: lisa:0026, lisa:0040, ana:0125

WARN · vague_opportunity
The opportunity ('use staged consent with re-contact points to maintain the researcher-participant relationship') duplicates I-01's opportunity almost verbatim and does not specifically address the 'relational betrayal' feeling described (e.g., co-ownership of knowledge, loss of partnership) — it's a generic consent-process fix bolted onto a distinct relational/ethical concern.

sections.name: I-06 · fail · Secondary reuse of qualitative data is rare

stickies.text:
I-06 · FAIL
Secondary reuse of qualitative data is rare

Secondary reuse is rare because researchers don't know how to find or evaluate existing qualitative datasets.

FAIL · bad_citation
nonexistent turns=[]; evidence_count=0

FAIL · unsupported
No turns cited to support the causal claim that reuse is rare specifically because researchers 'don't know how to find or evaluate' datasets.

FAIL · missing_counterexample
Sam — whose profile differs markedly from most interviewees (works at a research-intensive university with mature open-research infrastructure, professional open-research advocate) — directly contradicts this insight. He describes successfully browsing and reusing UK Data Service datasets by subject search and citing methods/questions from others' qualitative work. His account of a working discovery workflow is exactly the kind of counter-evidence that should be surfaced given the claim that reuse is 'rare' due to lack of know-how.

turns: sam:0065, sam:0068, sam:0069

WARN · merged_insights
The opportunity text is nearly identical to I-05's opportunity (publish qualitative-specific metadata standards/glossaries), collapsing two distinct problems — AV/multilingual de-identification difficulty (I-05) and discovery/evaluation of existing datasets for reuse (I-06) — into the same proposed fix, obscuring that these need different solutions (de-identification tooling and guidance vs. a searchable/quality-labelled discovery infrastructure).

sections.name: I-08 · fail · Funder mandates drive openness unevenly

stickies.text:
I-08 · FAIL
Funder mandates drive openness unevenly

Funder mandates drive openness unevenly — non-grant-funded sectors need sector-specific bodies (e.g. GSR) instead.

FAIL · bad_citation
nonexistent turns=[]; evidence_count=0

FAIL · unsupported
No turns cited.

turns: penni:0057, penni:0059, penni:0111

FAIL · overconfident
This insight is drawn essentially from a single participant (penni), whose comments were highly speculative and repeatedly hedged ('I don't know', 'it would have to come from GSR', 'maybe'). Presenting 'non-grant-funded sectors need sector-specific bodies (e.g. GSR) instead' as a settled finding overstates what was actually a tentative suggestion from one agency researcher who explicitly said she hadn't looked into it yet.

turns: penni:0057, penni:0059, penni:0111
